head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: cut[i] = min cuts for the first i characters; the starting value is the worst case (cut after every character, i−1); cut[0] = −1 so a palindrome starting at 0 costs 0
Initialising DP with the trivial upper bound
for l, r in ((c, c), (c, c + 1))
Two centres per index: odd-length (c,c) and even-length (c,c+1) palindromes
while l >= 0 and r < n and s[l] == s[r]
Grows the palindrome one character each side while it stays a palindrome
s[l..r] is a palindrome, so the prefix ending at r needs at most (best for prefix before l) + 1 cut
Relaxing a DP value from a discovered palindrome

p: `s = "aab"`. `cut` has n+1 entries; entry i is for the prefix of length i. Each row is one palindrome found:

blocks.h: Why expand around centres instead of testing all substrings?
p: Testing every substring for palindromeness costs O(n) each, O(n³) in total, or an O(n²) table. Expanding from each of the 2n−1 centres visits each palindrome once. The order is also safe: `cut[l]` depends only on palindromes ending before position `l`, and all of those have centres to the left of the current one, so they were processed earlier.

bullets: Time: O(n²), the total length of all expansions.
Space: O(n); no n×n palindrome table is needed.

132.takeaway: Min palindrome cuts: expand around each centre and relax cut[r+1] from cut[l]+1; O(n²) time with O(n) space.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Everyone starts with one candy (the minimum)
Left pass: a child rated above the left neighbour gets one more than that neighbour
Right pass: enforces the right-neighbour rule without breaking what the left pass guaranteed

p: A child must beat both neighbours when rated higher than both, and each pass only knows one side. The left pass fixes 'higher than left', the right pass fixes 'higher than right'. Taking `max` keeps the left-pass value where it already satisfies the right rule. Example `[1,2,3,2,1]`: the left pass gives `[1, 2, 3, 1, 1]`; the right pass raises the fourth child to 2 and keeps the peak at 3 thanks to `max`, giving `[1, 2, 3, 2, 1]`.

bullets: Time: O(n), two passes.
Space: O(n) for the candies array (an O(1) slope-counting version exists but is harder to explain).

135.takeaway: Two-pass greedy: satisfy the left-neighbour rule going right, the right-neighbour rule going left, and keep the max.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Dict from original node to its copy. Mapping None to None removes null checks later
Graph/list copying needs an old→new map
Creates the copy (nodes are hashable by identity)
Wires the copy's next to the copy of the original's next
Pass 2: wire links via the map
Same for random; works even when random points forward or backward

p: `A→B→C` with `A.random=C`, `B.random=A`, `C.random=B`:

A random pointer may point to a node that has not been copied yet (here `A.random = C`). If one pass created and wired nodes together, `clone[C]` would not exist when `A` is wired. Creating all copies first guarantees that every lookup in the second pass succeeds.

bullets: Time: O(n), two passes.
Space: O(n) for the dict. The interleaving trick (insert each copy after its original, wire random, then split) reaches O(1) extra space.

138.takeaway: Deep copy with random pointers: first create every copy in a hash map, then wire next and random through the map.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Gap between them grows by 1 per round
Fast reaches the end only if there is no cycle; the check protects `fast.next.next`
Null safety before a double step
Values may repeat in a list

p: `3 → 2 → 0 → -4`, with `-4` pointing back to `2`. Values shown are the node values the pointers sit on.

blocks.h: Why must they meet inside a cycle?
p: Once both are inside the cycle, fast gains exactly one step per round on slow, so the gap shrinks by 1 each round and cannot skip over 0 (it would have to jump by 2 to do so). They therefore meet within one lap of the cycle for slow.

bullets: Time: O(n). Slow enters the cycle after at most n steps, then the meeting takes at most the cycle length.
Space: O(1). A visited set also works but needs O(n).

141.takeaway: Floyd's tortoise and hare: a pointer moving twice as fast must catch the slow one if and only if there is a cycle.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: A list used as a stack, seeded with the root
Replacing recursion with an explicit stack
Takes the most recently added node (LIFO)
Visits the node immediately: preorder is 'node, left, right'
LIFO means the left child is popped first
Reversed push order to get the desired visit order

p: Tree `[1,null,2,3]` (1's right child is 2, whose left child is 3). The stack is shown bottom → top.

The stack returns items in reverse order of pushing. Pushing right first means left is on top and is processed (with its whole subtree, before right comes back up) next, which is exactly the left-before-right rule.

bullets: Time: O(n).
Space: O(h) for the stack in a balanced tree; up to O(n) for a skewed one. Morris traversal achieves O(1) by temporarily threading the tree.

144.takeaway: Iterative preorder: pop, visit, push right then left.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Substring test: true for a one-character operator. Note that `'-3'` is not a substring of `'+-*/'`, so negative numbers are treated as numbers
Pops the right operand first, then the left
True division then truncation toward zero, as the problem requires
The single value left at the end

p: Floor division rounds toward negative infinity, but Reverse Polish evaluation here must truncate toward zero. The two differ whenever the result is negative and inexact.

bullets: Time: O(n), one pass.
Space: O(n) for the stack (the number of operands waiting for an operator).

150.takeaway: A stack evaluates postfix: push numbers, and on an operator pop two operands (right first) and push the result.

What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Loop until one candidate is left (not `<=`, since `hi = mid` would never end)
Binary search that converges on a boundary
Compares mid with the right end, which reveals whether the rotation point is to the right
Comparing against hi avoids the ambiguity left comparison has
Right half excludes mid (it can't be the minimum); left half keeps mid (it might be)
lo == hi is the minimum's index

head: lo
hi
mid
nums[mid]
nums[hi]
decision
rows: nums[mid] > nums[hi]: min is right of mid → lo = mid+1
nums[mid] ≤ nums[hi]: min is at mid or left → hi = mid

bullets: Ends with `lo = hi = 3`, value `1`.

p: If `nums[mid] > nums[hi]` the sequence drops somewhere in `(mid, hi]`, so the minimum is to the right. Otherwise `[mid, hi]` is sorted and the minimum is at `mid` or to its left. Comparing with `lo` is ambiguous: on an array that is not rotated at all, `nums[mid] > nums[lo]` points right while the minimum is at index 0.

bullets: Time: O(log n).
Space: O(1).
Distinct values required; with duplicates `nums[mid] == nums[hi]` can't decide the side (the fix is `hi -= 1`).

153.takeaway: Binary search for the rotation point by comparing mid with the right end.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Saves the next node down the left spine before it is overwritten
New left child = the old right sibling of this node's parent
Remembers this node's right child for the next node down
New right child = the previous node (the old parent)
The last node on the spine is the new root

p: Tree `[1,2,3,4,5]`. Each row is after one node is processed; the last column is the sub-structure rooted at that node in `v(left,right)` form.

blocks.h: Why must the old `root.right` be saved before overwriting?
p: `root.right = prev` destroys the old right child, which has to become the *left* child of the next node down. The code therefore saves it in `prev_right` first and uses it one step later (`root.left = prev_right`). The order of the three assignments is the whole trick.

bullets: Time: O(h), only the left spine is walked.
Space: O(1). The recursive version uses O(h) stack.

156.takeaway: Upside-down tree: walk the left spine, and at each node rotate (parent becomes right child, right sibling becomes left child).

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Dict of character → occurrences inside the window; its size is the number of distinct characters
Sliding window with a distinct-count limit
Reads the count with a default of 0 (no KeyError)
Window invalid: more than two distinct characters
Drops the leftmost character; deleting at zero keeps `len(cnt)` equal to the distinct count
Essential, or the size never shrinks

p: `s = "eceba"`:

Removing one character from the left may not remove a whole distinct letter: with `aabbc` a single removal leaves `abbc`, which still has 3 distinct characters. The loop keeps shrinking until the window is valid again.
The condition `len(cnt) > 2` counts keys. If a count dropped to 0 but stayed in the dict, the window could never be recognised as valid again.

bullets: Time: O(n); `left` and `right` each move at most n times.
Space: O(1), at most 3 keys.

159.takeaway: Sliding window with a counts dict: grow right, and while distinct count exceeds the limit, shrink left (delete keys that hit zero).

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Reads the local slope at mid
Binary search on a property that is not sortedness
Going uphill: some peak must exist to the right (the array eventually ends or goes down)
Going downhill (or flat top): a peak exists at mid or to its left; keep mid
lo == hi is a peak index

head: lo
hi
mid
nums[mid] vs next
decision
rows: uphill: peak is right → lo = mid+1
downhill: peak at mid or left → hi = mid
uphill: peak is right → lo = mid+1

bullets: Ends at index `5` (value `6`).

blocks.h: Why does binary search work on an unsorted array?
p: The array doesn't need to be sorted, only to let us discard half with certainty. If `nums[mid] < nums[mid+1]` the sequence rises there, and following it right it must either keep rising to the last element (a peak, because `nums[n]` is treated as −∞) or turn down at some point (a peak). So a peak lies in `[mid+1, hi]`. The other case is symmetric. `mid + 1` is always a valid index because `mid < hi`.

bullets: Time: O(log n).
Space: O(1).
The code may return any peak, not necessarily the highest; the problem allows that. It relies on adjacent elements being distinct.

162.takeaway: Follow the slope: binary search on 'is the next element larger?' guarantees a peak in the half you keep.

What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Splits into a list of revision strings
Converts to a number: `'01'` becomes 1, `'10'` becomes 10; this is what makes the comparison numeric, not alphabetical
A missing revision counts as 0, so `1.0` equals `1.0.0`

blocks.h: Why compare as integers and not strings?
p: String comparison goes character by character, so `"2" > "10"`. Version fields are numbers, hence `int(...)`.

bullets: Time: O(n + m).
Space: O(n + m) for the split lists.

165.takeaway: Split on dots and compare revision by revision as integers, padding the shorter version with zeros.

What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Shifts from 1-based (A=1) to 0-based (A=0) digits before each division
Last digit of a base-26 number
Letter from a 0–25 value (65 is the code of 'A')
Moves to the next digit up
Digits were produced least significant first, so reverse

p: `701` → `"ZY"`. `n−1` is the value after the decrement:
bullets: Letters collected `Y`, `Z`; reversed: `ZY`.

p: Spreadsheet columns have no zero digit: A..Z are 1..26, then AA is 27. Plain base 26 would give 26 → '10'. Subtracting 1 turns the digits into 0..25 so `% 26` and `// 26` work, and the offset has to be applied on every iteration because every position is 1-based. Without it, 26 would produce `BA` instead of `Z`.

bullets: Time: O(log₂₆ n).
Space: O(log₂₆ n) for the letters.

168.takeaway: Excel titles are bijective base 26: decrement before each % and //, then reverse the letters.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: 1-based digits; no zero digit in this system
Horner's rule: shift left one base-26 place and add the next digit
Parsing a number in any base

p: Reading left to right, each new letter makes everything read so far one position more significant. Multiplying the running value by 26 and adding the new digit applies each place value once, with no need to compute 26^k or know the length in advance.

bullets: Time: O(L) for L letters.
Space: O(1).
This is the exact inverse of problem 168.

171.takeaway: Parse a bijective base-26 number with Horner's rule: n = n*26 + value.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Minimum health needed on entering cell (i, j) to survive to the end
One extra slot as a wall on the right; inf means 'cannot go that way'
Seeds the cell below the princess so that she needs just 1 HP to remain alive after her cell
Best of moving down (old value of need[j]) or right
Required HP before the cell; never below 1
A floor so health is never zero
Resets the wall after each row

p: `[[-2,-3,3],[-5,-10,1],[10,30,-5]]`, processed from the bottom row. `need` after each row (last entry is the wall):
bullets: Answer: `need[0] = 7`.

blocks.h: Why work backwards from the end?
p: Forward DP would need to track both current health and the minimum health seen so far, because a big bonus later cannot help if health already hit 0 earlier. Backwards, `need` is a single number per cell: the best option onward, minus this cell's effect, floored at 1.

bullets: Time: O(m·n).
Space: O(n), a single row.

174.takeaway: Dungeon Game is DP backwards from the goal: needed HP = max(1, min(next needs) − cell value).

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: In-place reversal with two converging pointers
Reversing a char list without extra space
Reverses the whole array: words come out in the right order but each is mirrored
The extra iteration at i == len(s) closes the last word, which has no trailing space
Next word starts after the space

p: `"the sky is blue"` as a character list:

Reversing the whole string puts the words in the desired order but spells each one backwards (`eulb si yks eht`). Reversing each word again restores the spelling. Together they are a rotation of whole words, in place and in two linear passes.

bullets: Time: O(n); each character is swapped at most twice.
Space: O(1). This is the point of the problem: the input is a mutable list, so no new string is built.

186.takeaway: Reverse words in place: reverse everything, then reverse each word.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Rotating by n is a no-op; this also makes k < n so `rev(0, k-1)` is valid
In-place reversal of nums[a..b] by swapping the ends inward
rev(0, n-1); rev(0, k-1); rev(k, n-1)
Three reversals that together rotate right by k

p: Reversing everything moves the last k items to the front, but backwards and with the rest also backwards. Reversing the first k and then the remaining n−k fixes each block's internal order. A shortcut `nums[:] = nums[-k:] + nums[:-k]` needs O(n) extra space.

bullets: Time: O(n); every element is moved at most twice.
Space: O(1).

p: When `k % n == 0`, `rev(0, -1)` does nothing and `rev(0, n-1)` runs twice, which restores the array, so the result is still correct.

189.takeaway: Rotate in place with three reversals: all, first k, rest.

DP that depends on the last two states
Rob this house: add its value to the best that skipped the previous house
Choose the better of skipping or robbing this house
Tuple assignment: the right side is evaluated first with the old values, so no temp variable is needed

cur = max(old cur, old prev + x)
prev after
cur after

blocks.h: Why is it enough to keep two numbers?
p: `dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i])` reads only the last two entries. Keeping `prev` and `cur` replaces the whole table, cutting space from O(n) to O(1). The `max` encodes the adjacency rule: robbing house i means house i−1 was skipped, so it builds on `dp[i-2]`.

bullets: Time: O(n).
Space: O(1).

198.takeaway: House Robber: dp[i] = max(skip, rob + dp[i-2]), compressed to two variables.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Shifts right by one bit, discarding the lowest bit
Shifts left to put the common prefix back in its original position
Loop until both numbers equal their common binary prefix
Finding the common prefix of two numbers

bullets: Common prefix `1` shifted left by 2 is `100` = 4.

blocks.h: Why is the answer the common prefix?
p: Between `left` and `right` every count passes through, so any bit position where the two numbers differ (and everything below it) takes both values 0 and 1 somewhere in the range. The AND is therefore 0 in all those positions. Above the first differing bit, all numbers in the range share the same bits, and the AND keeps them. Shifting right until both are equal finds exactly that shared prefix.

bullets: Time: O(log n), at most one iteration per bit.
Space: O(1).

201.takeaway: Range AND equals the common binary prefix of the endpoints; strip differing bits with shifts and shift back.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Marking numbers, a sieve of Eratosthenes
Only primes up to √n need to cross off multiples, since a composite below n has a factor ≤ √n
Starts crossing off at i², because smaller multiples (2i, 3i, …) were already crossed by smaller primes

p: `n = 10` (counts primes strictly less than 10). Rows show which numbers each prime crosses off:
bullets: Primes below 10: 2, 3, 5, 7, so the answer is 4.

blocks.h: Why start at i² and stop at √n?
p: A composite number c < n has a smallest prime factor p with p² ≤ c, so it gets crossed off by p starting at p². Everything below p² that is a multiple of p has a smaller prime factor and is already gone. This cuts the work to O(n log log n).

bullets: Time: O(n log log n).
Space: O(n) for the boolean array.
`n < 3` returns 0 early because there is no prime below 2.

204.takeaway: Sieve of Eratosthenes: cross off multiples of each prime starting at i², up to √n.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Adjacency list: course → courses that depend on it. Missing keys give an empty list
Counts how many prerequisites a course still waits on
deque(i for i in … if indeg[i] == 0)
Queue seeded with courses that have no prerequisites
Takes a ready course in FIFO order
Finishing a course unlocks dependents whose last prerequisite it was
Every course was processed; if not, some are stuck in a cycle

p: 4 courses, prerequisites `[[1,0],[2,0],[3,1],[3,2]]` (course 3 needs 1 and 2; both need 0):

blocks.h: Why does `done == n` detect a cycle?
p: Courses on a cycle always wait for each other, so their indegree never reaches 0 and they are never enqueued. The count of processed courses then stays below n. With no cycle there is always a course with indegree 0, so all n get processed.

bullets: Time: O(V + E), each course and each prerequisite edge is handled once.
Space: O(V + E) for the graph.

207.takeaway: Kahn's topological sort: repeatedly process zero-indegree courses; if you can't process all of them, there's a cycle.
